questions.question: Which chain draws a red background that does NOT extend into the 16 dp padding?
options: Modifier.padding(16.dp).background(Color.Red)
Modifier.background(Color.Red).padding(16.dp)
Either: modifier order doesn't change the result
Modifier.background(Color.Red).size(16.dp)
questions.explanation: Modifiers apply from left to right, each wrapping what follows. Padding first shrinks the area, and the background is then drawn only inside it. With `background` first, the background covers the full size and the padding is applied inside it, so the red extends under the padding.

questions.question: When does the block inside `LaunchedEffect(Unit) { ... }` run?
options: Once on entering the composition; cancelled when it leaves
On every recomposition of the composable that contains it
Every time the hosting Activity comes back to the RESUMED state
Once per app process, no matter how many times it is composed
questions.explanation: `LaunchedEffect` launches a coroutine when it enters the composition and cancels it when it leaves. It only restarts when one of its keys changes, and `Unit` never changes. It is tied to the composition, not to Activity lifecycle callbacks or the process.

questions.question: In Compose's layout phase a parent may measure each child only once per pass; trying to measure the same child twice throws an exception.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Compose enforces single-pass measurement so that deep layouts stay linear in cost, unlike nested weights in Views. A layout that needs information before measuring uses intrinsic measurements or `SubcomposeLayout` instead. Calling `measure` twice on the same measurable throws.

questions.question: The user types "kotlin" quickly, one character at a time. What happens?
options: Each new query cancels the running effect and starts another, acting as a debounce
The effects queue up and run one after another, one search for every character typed
Only the first query runs; later changes to query are ignored by the running effect
All of the effects run in parallel, and whichever search finishes last sets results
questions.explanation: When a `LaunchedEffect` key changes, Compose cancels the old coroutine and launches a new one. Each keystroke cancels the previous effect during its `delay`, so only the final query, after 300 ms without typing, actually searches. Effects never queue or run in parallel for the same call site.

questions.question: After 2 s the parent recomposes and passes a new `onTimeout` lambda. Which lambda is called when the 5 s are up?
options: The first: the effect captured it and was never restarted
The new one, since effects always see the latest parameters
Neither: the effect is cancelled when a parameter changes
Both of them, the old one first and then the new one
questions.explanation: The `LaunchedEffect` keyed on `Unit` keeps running with the lambda captured when it started, so it calls a stale callback. Changing a parameter only restarts an effect if it is one of its keys. Use `val current by rememberUpdatedState(onTimeout)` and call `current()` so the timer keeps running but invokes the latest lambda.

questions.question: When does `onDispose` run here? Select all that apply.
options: When the composable leaves the composition
When lifecycleOwner changes, before the effect re-runs
After every recomposition of the composable
Whenever the Activity receives onStop
questions.explanation: `DisposableEffect` cleans up when it leaves the composition and whenever a key changes, running `onDispose` before starting again with the new key. That is what makes this safe if a different `LifecycleOwner` is passed. It does not run on ordinary recompositions or follow Activity callbacks.

questions.question: Which of these use a side-effect API correctly? Select all that apply.
options: `rememberCoroutineScope()` to launch a scroll animation from onClick
`LaunchedEffect` called inside onClick to start work on each tap
`SideEffect { }` to push current state to a non-Compose object after composition
`produceState` to expose a suspending or callback source as State
`DisposableEffect` with no `onDispose` block to add a listener
questions.explanation: Event handlers are not composable, so they use a coroutine scope from `rememberCoroutineScope`; calling `LaunchedEffect` in `onClick` does not compile. `SideEffect` runs after every successful composition, which suits syncing state outward, and `produceState` turns a source into State. A `DisposableEffect` block must end with `onDispose`, or it does not compile.

questions.question: Why is the lambda version preferred when `scrollOffset` changes every frame?
options: The lambda reads state during layout, so frames re-layout instead of recomposing
The lambda version runs on a background thread, so it no longer blocks the main thread
They're the same: the lambda is only syntax sugar for the value-based offset overload
The value version is faster because it doesn't allocate a new lambda on every frame
questions.explanation: Compose has three phases: composition, layout and drawing. Passing `scrollOffset.dp` reads the state during composition, so each change recomposes the composable; the lambda overload defers the read to the placement step, so only layout reruns. Everything still runs on the main thread, and the lambda is not re-created each frame.

questions.question: How do you make the divider exactly as tall as the taller of the two texts, without hard-coding a height?
options: Give the Row Modifier.height(IntrinsicSize.Min)
Measure the Texts twice in a custom Layout first
Put Modifier.wrapContentHeight() on the divider
Put Modifier.weight(1f) on the divider instead
questions.explanation: `fillMaxHeight` fills whatever the Row allows, and a plain Row's height is not known before its children are measured. `IntrinsicSize.Min` asks the children for their intrinsic heights before measuring, so the Row gets the tallest text's height and the divider fills exactly that. Measuring children twice is not allowed, and `weight` acts on the Row's main (horizontal) axis.

questions.question: In a `LazyColumn` whose `items` have no `key`, `remember`ed state belongs to a position, so inserting an item at the top can make that state appear on the wrong row.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Without keys, lazy items are identified by their index, so after an insert at index 0 each row inherits the remembered state (expanded flags, text input) of whatever used to be at its position. Passing `key = { it.id }` ties state to the item itself, and also lets the list keep scroll position and animate moves correctly.
